newsitem.title: BELARUS: Belarus's Lukashenko wants to rule for decade.
newsitem.headline: Belarus's Lukashenko wants to rule for decade.

text.p: Hardline Belarussian President Alexander Lukashenko, pushing a proposed new constitution that would extend his powers, said on Friday that he intended to rule his former Soviet republic for another 10 years.
Lukashenko also told a session of parliament that he would proceed with a referendum on the constitution, scheduled to be held on November 7, anniversary of the Bolshevik revolution.
"As regards your fears about prolonging my powers... Lukashenko will be president for a total of 12 years," he told the chamber.
Lukashenko became Belarus's first post-Soviet president two years ago on a platform of fighting corruption and pressing for a union of some sort with neighbouring Russia.
Under the new constitution, the president may be elected for two five-year terms. Lukashenko's comments indicated he intended to start a full new mandate if the draft wins approval.

The text calls for a new upper house of parliament, with a third of its members named by the president, who would also be empowered to dissolve the assembly, call plebiscites at will and appoint members of the constitutional court and heads of local government.
Lukashenko's rule has become increasingly authoritarian in recent months.
Up to 200 people have been given short jail terms for taking part in mass demonstrations last spring against his signing of a pact that would create a "community" with Russia.
On Thursday, seven extreme nationalists from Belarus's southern neighbour, Ukraine, were given sentences of one to three years on more serious public order charges connected with the protests.
Two opposition politicians were granted political asylum in the United States in August after fleeing the country.
The president's crackdowns have also focused on the press, with several editors sacked and a number of newspapers closed down or forced to publish abroad.
An independent radio station in the capital Minsk was shut down last week by government order and the bank accounts of several independent newspapers were closed.
Since publication of the draft constitution last week, Lukashenko has said he will produce a different text.

He intends to put three other questions to a referendum to secure a ban on private land ownership, entrench the death penalty and change the post-Soviet national holiday to honour the World War Two recapture of Minsk by Red Army troops.
Deputies oppose the referendums, saying the results are a foregone conclusion given Lukashenko's tight control over electronic media.
